logline: Anti-corruption detectives inside a fictional UK police force relentlessly pursue bent colleagues, each series built around one suspected officer and a conspiracy that grows wider with every interrogation.

bollymeter.basis: 100 percent on Rotten Tomatoes; the debut series announced Jed Mercurio's procedural grip and Martin Compston's straight-arrow Arnott as an immediately compelling lead.

seasons.review_body: The debut five-episode series aired on BBC Two in summer 2012 and earned a perfect Rotten Tomatoes score. Critics identified an immediately distinct procedural grammar: AC-12's under-resourced investigators targeting a corrupt armed-response officer, with Jed Mercurio's writing foregrounding the bureaucratic detail of internal investigations rather than standard chase-and-catch plotting. The central dynamic between DS Arnott (Martin Compston) and Superintendent Hastings (Adrian Dunbar) was praised for its ambiguity - Hastings reads as either a principled leader or a man with something to hide, and the show refuses to resolve the question cheaply.

bollymeter.basis: 100 percent on Rotten Tomatoes; Keeley Hawes's DI Lindsay Denton was cited as one of British television's great morally ambiguous characters.

seasons.review_body: Series 2 aired in early 2014 on BBC Two and held the perfect Rotten Tomatoes critical mark. Keeley Hawes joined as DI Lindsay Denton, the officer under AC-12 scrutiny, and her performance drew near-universal praise for sustaining genuine ambiguity across six episodes: critics could not agree whether she was corrupt, compromised, or simply unlucky. The interrogation scenes that became the show's signature device - two detectives, a table, a solicitor, and a spiralling disclosure - reached a new intensity level in this series. Audience engagement and broadcast figures grew substantially over Series 1.
seasons.season_over_season: Series 2 introduced the anthological-suspect structure that became the show's template, and Keeley Hawes's performance set the benchmark for all subsequent central targets.

bollymeter.basis: 100 percent on Rotten Tomatoes; the introduction of DS Kate Fleming and the expanding conspiracy narrative deepened the show's mythology without sacrificing season-level satisfaction.

seasons.review_body: Series 3 moved to BBC One and landed another perfect critical score on Rotten Tomatoes. The series introduced a wider criminal conspiracy within the police, centered on "the fourth man" and an organized crime group (OCG), building mythology that carried across the remaining series. Vicky McClure's DS Kate Fleming was now a full co-lead alongside Compston, with the show developing a genuine repertory ensemble. The jump to BBC One also scaled up its reach, reinforcing its status as a prestige flagship drama in British television.
seasons.season_over_season: The move to BBC One and the introduction of long-arc conspiracy mythology raised both the scale and the audience, without losing the procedural precision of earlier series.

bollymeter.basis: 100 percent on Rotten Tomatoes; Thandiwe Newton's DCI Roz Huntley brought a new register of moral complexity to the suspect role.

seasons.review_body: Series 4 maintains a perfect critical record with Thandiwe Newton as DCI Roz Huntley, the season’s central suspect. Newton’s performance stands out for its calculating, compartmentalised control, paired with sudden vulnerability in key moments. The AC-12 procedural mechanics are now familiar, so Mercurio’s scripts emphasize how institutional corruption operates as a system rather than as isolated misconduct, while still sustaining episode-level tension through the interrogation sequences. The fourth consecutive 100 percent Rotten Tomatoes score confirms the show as one of the strongest long-running procedural series on British television.
seasons.season_over_season: Thandiwe Newton’s guest lead matches that high bar, sustaining the perfect critical record into a fourth year.

bollymeter.basis: 90 percent on Rotten Tomatoes; Stephen Graham's DS John Corbett storyline was praised as the show's most emotionally complex arc, though some critics felt the conspiracy plotting had grown unwieldy.

seasons.review_body: Series 5 aired in spring 2019 and registered the show’s first drop from a perfect Rotten Tomatoes score, settling at 90 percent. The series featured Stephen Graham as an undercover officer, and the mythology built across four prior years now left the narrative threads to grapple with longer accumulation. Praise centered on Graham’s performance and on the emotional toll Mercurio’s writing placed on the central trio. The conspiracy’s internal logic began to strain. Audience numbers remained enormous, with the show among the most watched dramas in BBC history, while the audience score on Rotten Tomatoes held at 94 percent overall.
seasons.season_over_season: Stephen Graham's emotionally rich arc pushed the show toward new dramatic territory while the accumulated conspiracy weight began to create structural pressure that critics began to flag.

bollymeter.basis: 86 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 25 reviews; the resolution of the multi-series 'H' mystery proved divisive, with The Guardian giving it three stars and the New Statesman calling it a whimper.

pull_quotes.text: It was all fine. But, oh my, you should have seen it when it was good.

seasons.review_body: Series 6 opened in March 2021 to record BBC figures - 9.6 million viewers for the premiere - but the finale sparked the most divided critical response in the show's run. The long-teased resolution of the 'H' four-man conspiracy and the identity of the mysterious fourth OCG member landed at 86 percent on Rotten Tomatoes, with the Guardian giving the finale three stars and Lucy Mangan writing: 'It was all fine. But, oh my, you should have seen it when it was good.' The New Statesman called it a series that 'ended with a whimper, not a bang.' The Times was kinder, awarding four stars. Audience disappointment was measurable in social media response; the scale of the finale's scrutiny reflected how much viewer investment the show had accumulated over a decade.
seasons.season_over_season: The payoff series for a nine-year conspiracy arc polarised critics, with the deflating 'H' reveal pushing the show's critical score below 90 percent for the first time.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 7
episode_reviews.review_body: Line of Duty Series 6 Episode 7 aired May 2, 2021 on BBC One as the finale of the most-watched series in the show's history - Series 6's premiere drew 9.6 million viewers - and the most debated episode in its decade-long run. The Guardian's Lucy Mangan, in a three-star review, wrote: 'It was all fine. But, oh my, you should have seen it when it was good.' The New Statesman called it a series that 'ended with a whimper, not a bang.' The Times awarded four stars. The 86-percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 25 critics reflects the genuine critical division: the reveal of 'H' - the fourth corrupt officer whose identity the show had been building toward since Series 3 - was described by defenders as credibly mundane, a statement about institutional corruption's banality rather than its drama, and by disappointed viewers as an anti-climactic payoff to nine years of audience theorising. The interrogation room sequence that delivers the revelation operates at the show's procedural standard. The bollymeter of 6.5 reflects an episode that performed its function adequately while failing to satisfy the emotional investment the preceding decade had accumulated.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The series finale delivers the long-awaited identity of the fourth man and closes out AC-12's decade-long conspiracy investigation. Critics were split down the middle: those who found the resolution credibly mundane praised its realism; those who had followed the mythology for years felt the reveal deflated rather than paid off a ten-year investment.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The interrogation room reveal of 'H' - the culmination of six years of fan theorising.
